input.question: I understand from the news that if we don't bomb Syria our reputation will take a major hit internationally. Why do we care about our reputation internationally?
input.ground_truth: Our President warned publicly that the use of chemical weapons (weapons of mass destruction) against civilians would constitute a dangerous line to cross in escalating the conflict. Syria used them anyway, in a blatant manner which couldn't avoid notice. Therefore the President has to make it clear that such warnings are not in vain; there will be some sort of consequence from violating such a warning, otherwise future warnings can be ignored as toothless (re: North Korea).

Question: I understand from the news that if we don't bomb Syria our reputation will take a major hit internationally. Why do we care about our reputation internationally?

Okay, let's imagine countries are like kids in a big playground. When you play nicely and follow the rules, the other kids think you are a good friend. They want to play with you and trust you. If you break the rules or don’t help when you should, the other kids might not want to play with you anymore. They might think you’re not a good friend.

So, when a country like the United States does things that other countries think are right, other countries want to be friends and work with them. If the US does something that seems mean or unfair, like bombing another country without a good reason, the other countries might not trust the US anymore. They might not want to work with the US or help them in the future.

That’s why the US cares about its “reputation” on the world playground—it wants to be someone everyone likes and trusts.
